summary: The note explains seismic intensity scales, which rate the severity of ground shaking at a location, as distinct from magnitude scales that measure an earthquake's overall strength. It covers how shaking intensity depends on source size, wave type, depth, distance and local soil conditions, and how isoseismal maps are used. It also traces the history of intensity scales from the 1780s to the Modified Mercalli and MSK-64 scales and lists the scales used in various countries and regions.
one_line: Overview of seismic intensity scales that rate earthquake ground shaking, their factors, history, and the scales used in different countries.
key_facts: Seismic intensity scales categorize the intensity or severity of ground shaking at a given location, while seismic magnitude scales measure the overall strength of an earthquake.
Intensity scales are based on observed effects, such as the degree to which people or animals were alarmed and the extent and severity of damage to structures or natural features.
Site response can amplify ground motions as much as ten times, especially where unconsolidated sediments lie in a basin.
In the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, the Marina district of San Francisco was one of the most damaged areas, though it was nearly 100 km from the epicenter.
The first simple classification of earthquake intensity was devised by Domenico Pignataro in the 1780s.
The first recognisable intensity scale in the modern sense was drawn up by P.N.G. Egen in 1828.

Robert Mallet, an Irish engineer sent by Imperial College, London, made the first modern mapping of earthquake intensity for the December 1857 Basilicata earthquake, also known as The Great Neapolitan Earthquake of 1857.
The first widely adopted intensity scale, the Rossi–Forel scale, was introduced in the late 19th century as a 10 grade scale.
In 1902, Italian seismologist Giuseppe Mercalli created the Mercalli Scale, a new 12-grade scale.
Charles Francis Richter found during the 1950s a correlation between seismic intensity and peak ground acceleration (PGA) for California.
Richter's relation for California is log a = I/3 − 0.5, where a is the PGA at a site in cm/sec and I is the intensity value for that site.
The Modified Mercalli intensity scale (MMS) incorporates building vulnerability types, and the European MSK-64 scale also added this quantitative element.
Where an earthquake is not recorded on seismographs, an isoseismal map of felt intensities can be used to estimate its location and magnitude.
In Japan, isoseismal-type information is used when an earthquake occurs to anticipate the severity of damage in different areas.
The Modified Mercalli scale is used in the United States, Hong Kong and Indonesia, while the Medvedev–Sponheuer–Karnik scale is used in India, Israel, Kazakhstan and Russia.
The USGS ShakeMap provides near-real-time maps of ground motion and shaking intensity following significant earthquakes.
